\chapter{Un and Una --- the Other Article}
\label{ch:spanish-indefinite-article}
\hlchaptermodality{3}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say a day, an afternoon and a night, choosing the article by the noun's gender.}

un is the number one, and English a is the same word worn down.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[un]{un — \textquotedblleft{}a,\textquotedblright{} and the number hiding in it}

\label{lesson:ES-C02-un}



\begin{quote}
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}the day\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{El día}.) Which word is doing the work of \emph{the}? (\emph{El}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the other article}]
\emph{El día} is \textbf{the} day — a particular one, the one we both know about.

For \textbf{a} day, any day, not one we have settled on, Spanish swaps the article:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{un día} — \emph{a day.}
\end{quote}

That is the second article, and Spanish has only these two kinds. \emph{El} points at something known; \textbf{un} does not.

Like \emph{el}, it carries the noun's gender — so \emph{un} is the masculine one, and its partner is coming in the next lesson.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Here is the part worth keeping.

\textbf{Un is the number one.} Latin \emph{ūnus}, \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{}, and Spanish never really separated the two — \emph{un día} is \emph{a day} and \emph{one day} at once, and context decides which you meant.

\textbf{English did exactly the same thing and hid it better.} Our \emph{a} and \emph{an} are the word \textbf{one}, worn down over centuries of being unstressed. That is why \emph{an hour} and \emph{one hour} start with the same sound, and why \emph{a} feels like almost nothing when you say it: it has been eroded from a whole number down to a single vowel.

So the two languages made the same move. Spanish just left the seam visible.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el día\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}un día\textquotedblright{} — the known one, then any one
  \item \textquotedblleft{}un día\textquotedblright{}, and hear the number \emph{one} still sitting in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}a day\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Un día}.) What is the difference between \emph{el} and \emph{un}? (\emph{El} points at something known; \emph{un} does not.) And what number is \emph{un}? (\textbf{One} — and English \emph{a} is the same word.) Next: the feminine partner.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[una]{una — the feminine one}

\label{lesson:ES-C02-una}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}a day.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Un día}.) And what is the word for \textquotedblleft{}the afternoon\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{La tarde}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the partner}]
\emph{Tarde} and \emph{noche} are feminine, so they take the feminine article:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{una tarde} — \emph{an afternoon.} \textbf{una noche} — \emph{a night.}
\end{quote}

You now have both, and they behave exactly as \emph{el} and \emph{la} do — the article takes the gender of the noun standing next to it. Nothing new is being asked of you; the rule you learned for \emph{el} and \emph{la} simply applies again.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{masculine} & \textbf{feminine} \\
\midrule
the & \emph{el} día & \emph{la} tarde \\
a & \textbf{un} día & \textbf{una} tarde \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

This table is allowed here because every box in it is something you can already say.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
One detail, because it runs against what you might expect.

\emph{Una} is not \emph{un} with something added. It is the other way round: Latin had \emph{ūnus} and \emph{ūna}, and \textbf{una kept the whole word while un lost a syllable.}

That is the ordinary direction of travel. The forms said most often wear down fastest, and \emph{un} — standing in front of masculine nouns, which are the default for anything unspecified — got said more.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}un día, una tarde, una noche\textquotedblright{}
  \item each noun twice — once with \emph{the}, once with \emph{a}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}a night.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Una noche}.) Which article goes with \emph{día}, and why? (\textbf{Un} — \emph{día} is masculine.) And which of the pair is the worn-down one? (\textbf{Un} — \emph{una} kept the whole Latin word.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Review — the four little words}

\label{lesson:ES-C02-repaso-articulos}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new here. Say \textquotedblleft{}the day,\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}a day.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four words, and they cover every noun you will ever meet in this book:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{el} · \textbf{la} — \emph{the}, pointing at something we both know.
  \item \textbf{un} · \textbf{una} — \emph{a}, pointing at no one in particular.
\end{itemize}

Two jobs, two genders, and the gender is never the article's own — it is borrowed from the noun beside it, exactly as \emph{bueno} borrowed it from \emph{día}.

That is one rule doing all four jobs, and you have now seen it three times: on the greeting, on the definite article, and here.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}el día, un día\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}la tarde, una tarde\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}la noche, una noche\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Until the article arrives with the noun rather than after it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name all four articles. (\emph{El}, \emph{la}, \emph{un}, \emph{una}.) Which two point at something known? (\emph{El} and \emph{la}.) And where does an article's gender come from? (\textbf{The noun beside it} — never from itself.)
\end{tcolorbox}
